stem:
Draw the product of this {{SN2}} reaction and show its stereochemistry. Label the starting material and the product R or S.
[[rxn:[2H][C@H](CCC)Br + [SH-].[Na+]>DMSO;>"product"]]
model:
[[rxn:[2H][C@H](CCC)Br + [SH-].[Na+]>DMSO;>[2H][C@@H](CCC)S + [Na+].[Br-]]]

Starting material: R. Product: S. The sulfur attacks the carbon from the side opposite the bromine in one step, so the configuration is inverted.

rubric.h: SH is on the carbon that carried Br, and Br is gone
The product is drawn with the opposite configuration at that carbon (inversion), with D shown
Starting material labelled R and product labelled S
Says backside attack or inversion, or shows NaBr as the by-product

steps.t: Find the leaving group and its carbon
steps.h: Bromide is the leaving group. Its carbon carries Br, D, H and a propyl chain: four different groups, so it is a stereocentre. It is a primary carbon, which is open to backside attack.

ask.q: Why is this carbon a stereocentre when it has two hydrogens?
ask.a: One of them is deuterium. H and D count as different groups.

steps.h: {{HS-}} attacks with sulfur. It is one of the best nucleophiles in the lecture table (126,000).
Sulfur comes in on the side opposite bromine. In the transition state S, C and Br are on one line and the propyl chain, D and H are in one plane.

ask.q: From which side does the sulfur approach?
ask.a: From the side directly opposite the C-Br bond.

steps.h:
Keep the chain where it is and put SH on the carbon with the opposite kind of bond to the one Br had. D and H have swapped sides relative to the chain.
[[mol:[2H][C@@H](CCC)S]]

Starting material: Br > propyl carbon > D > H gives R. Product: SH > propyl carbon > D > H gives S. Here the nucleophile takes the same rank the leaving group had, so the label changes with the geometry.

ask.q: Does D rank above or below H?
ask.a: Above. Deuterium has the higher mass.

steps.h: Sodium bromide.

solution.rule: SN2 puts the nucleophile on the face opposite the leaving group: inversion.

stem:
cis-1-Bromo-3-methylcyclohexane is treated with NaCN in DMSO. What is the major product?
[[ring:1u:Br,3u:CH3]]

choices.why: CN is on the face opposite the one Br left from, and the methyl group has not moved: trans.
This is retention: CN sits exactly where Br was. A nucleophile cannot enter through the leaving group.
A mixture of both faces would need a planar carbocation ({{SN1}}). With a good nucleophile in DMSO the reaction is {{SN2}}, which gives one product.
This is elimination. Cyanide is a good nucleophile and a weak base, so it substitutes.

steps.h: Br and {{CH3}} are both on wedges, so they are cis. The carbon with Br is secondary and bromide is a good leaving group.

ask.a: Carbon 1, the one bonded to Br.

steps.h: Cyanide is a good nucleophile and DMSO is a polar aprotic solvent: the conditions for {{SN2}}.
Cyanide attacks carbon 1 from the face opposite Br. Br was up, so CN ends up down.

ask.a: No. Carbon 3 is not touched, so its wedge stays a wedge.

steps.h:
CN down and {{CH3}} up are on opposite faces: the product is trans.
[[ring:1d:CN,3u:CH3]]

solution.answer: trans-3-Methylcyclohexanecarbonitrile (CN on a dash, methyl still on a wedge).
solution.rule: On a ring, SN2 turns the wedge at the attacked carbon into a dash: cis becomes trans.

stem:
Draw the product of this reaction with its stereochemistry and give its R or S label.
[[rxn:CC[C@@H](C)OS(=O)(=O)c1ccc(C)cc1 + CC(=O)[O-].[Na+]>DMF;>"product"]]
model:
[[rxn:CC[C@@H](C)OS(=O)(=O)c1ccc(C)cc1 + CC(=O)[O-].[Na+]>DMF;>CC[C@H](C)OC(C)=O + Cc1ccc(S(=O)(=O)[O-])cc1.[Na+]]]

The tosylate (R) gives the acetate with the opposite configuration (S). The acetate oxygen attacks the carbon from the side opposite the C-OTs bond.

rubric.h: Product is an ester: the stereocentre is bonded to an acetate oxygen and the OTs group is gone
The new C-O bond is on the opposite face to the old one (inversion)
Tosylate (TsO-) shown as the leaving group

steps.h: The leaving group is the whole tosylate, {{TsO-}}. The bond that breaks is the C-O bond between the stereocentre and the tosylate oxygen.

ask.q: Which bond breaks: C-O or O-S?
ask.a: C-O. The oxygen leaves with the sulfur as {{TsO-}}.

steps.h: Acetate attacks with a negatively charged oxygen (lecture table: 630). The carbon is secondary, and acetate is a weak base, so the reaction is {{SN2}}.

The new C-O bond to acetate goes on the face opposite the C-OTs bond: if the tosylate is drawn on a wedge, the acetate is drawn on a dash, and the other way round. The ethyl and methyl groups stay put.

ask.q: Is the oxygen now on the stereocentre the same oxygen as before?
ask.a: No. It is an acetate oxygen. The old one left with the tosylate.

steps.h: Starting material: OTs > ethyl > methyl > H gives R. Product: O > ethyl > methyl > H with the opposite geometry gives S.
Sodium tosylate, {{NaOTs}}.

solution.answer: (S)-butan-2-yl acetate, formed with inversion, plus NaOTs.
solution.rule: A tosylate leaves as a whole group: the C-O bond breaks and the nucleophile enters from the back.

stem:
(S)-2-Bromo-1-methoxypropane reacts with NaCN in DMSO. Which answer gives the correct product and the correct label?
[[mol:COC[C@H](C)Br]]

choices.why: CN is on the opposite face (inversion), and because {{CH2OCH3}} now outranks CN the label stays S.
The drawing is right, but the label was guessed from the rule that S becomes R. Ranking the groups again gives S.
This drawing has CN on the same face Br was on, which is retention. It was chosen to make the letter change.

choices.h: A racemic mixture of both nitriles
choices.why: Racemization needs a carbocation ({{SN1}}). A good nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent reacts by {{SN2}}.

steps.h:
Secondary carbon, bromide leaving group, cyanide in DMSO: {{SN2}} with inversion. Put CN on the face opposite the one Br occupied.
[[mol:COC[C@@H](C)C#N]]

ask.q: Which do you settle first, the drawing or the label?
ask.a: The drawing. The label is read from the finished drawing.

steps.t: Rank the groups in the starting material
steps.h: Br > {{CH2OCH3}} > {{CH3}} > H. The leaving group is rank 1.

steps.t: Rank the groups in the product
steps.h: The CN carbon carries (N, N, N). The {{CH2OCH3}} carbon carries (O, H, H). Compare the first point of difference: O beats N, so {{CH2OCH3}} > CN > {{CH3}} > H. The nucleophile is only rank 2.

ask.a: {{CH2OCH3}}: oxygen beats nitrogen at the first point of difference.

steps.h: The geometry inverted and ranks 1 and 2 traded places. The two changes cancel, so the label is still S.
Inversion happened. The letter did not change. Both statements are true together.

ask.q: Does an unchanged letter mean retention?
ask.a: No. R and S depend on priorities. Inversion is about which face the new group is on.

solution.answer: The inverted nitrile, and it is still called S.
solution.rule: Inversion is geometry. Assign R or S afresh, because the priorities can change.

stem:
What is the product of this reaction?
[[rxn:[2H][C@H](C)Cl + [OH-].[Na+]>>"?"]]

choices.why: OH is on the face opposite the one Cl left from: inversion, the (S) alcohol, exactly the lecture example.
Retention: OH drawn where Cl was. Backside attack puts it on the other face.
A racemic mixture comes from a carbocation. A primary carbocation does not form, and {{SN2}} gives one enantiomer.
This is elimination. On an unhindered primary carbon, hydroxide substitutes.

steps.h: A primary carbon with a good leaving group and hydroxide, a strong nucleophile: {{SN2}}.
OH goes on the face opposite Cl. D and H swap sides relative to the methyl group.
Cl > {{CH3}} > D > H gives R for the chloride. O > {{CH3}} > D > H with the inverted geometry gives S.

solution.rule: One enantiomer in, one enantiomer out, inverted.

stem:
trans-1-Bromo-4-methylcyclohexane is heated with NaCN in DMSO. What is the substitution product?
[[ring:1u:Br,4d:CH3]]

choices.why: CN is on the face opposite the one Br occupied. Both groups are now down: cis.
Retention: this is still trans, with CN in the place of Br.
Both faces would be attacked only if a planar carbocation formed ({{SN1}}).
This is elimination. Cyanide is a good nucleophile and a weak base, so it substitutes.

steps.h: Br up, {{CH3}} down: trans.
CN enters carbon 1 from below, opposite Br, so CN is down.
CN down and {{CH3}} down are on the same face: cis.

solution.rule: Trans becomes cis, cis becomes trans.

stem:
Draw the product, with stereochemistry, and label it R or S.
[[rxn:CC[C@H](C)I + [N-]=[N+]=[N-].[Na+]>DMF;>"product"]]

rubric.h: {{N3}} is on carbon 2 and iodine is gone
Opposite configuration to the starting material (inversion)

steps.h: Iodide is the leaving group on a secondary stereocentre. Azide, {{N3-}}, is a good nucleophile (lecture table: 8,000) and DMF is polar aprotic: {{SN2}}.
The azide nitrogen bonds to the same carbon on the face opposite iodine: if iodine is drawn on a wedge, the azide goes on a dash, and the other way round.
Starting material: I > ethyl > methyl > H gives S. Product: N > ethyl > methyl > H with inverted geometry gives R.

solution.rule: Nucleophile in from the back, leaving group out the front.

choices.why: SH is on the opposite face to the old OTs group, so it is now cis to the methyl group.
Retention: SH is drawn where OTs was, still trans.
This breaks the O-S bond and leaves the oxygen on the ring. In a tosylate the C-O bond breaks and the whole OTs group leaves.
Elimination. {{HS-}} is an excellent nucleophile and a weak base, so substitution wins.

steps.h: The methyl group and the OTs group are on opposite faces of the five-membered ring: trans.
The ring C-O bond. Tosylate leaves as {{TsO-}}, and sulfur attacks the ring carbon.
SH ends up on the face opposite the one OTs was on, which is the face the methyl group is on: cis.

solution.rule: Trans tosylate, cis product: the attacked carbon inverts and its neighbour does not.

stem:
(S)-Butane-2-thiol is wanted from a 2-bromobutane and NaSH in DMSO. Which starting material gives it?
[[mol:CC[C@H](C)S]]

choices.why: The (R) bromide has Br on the opposite face. Backside attack by {{HS-}} gives the (S) thiol.
The (S) bromide would give the (R) thiol. This choice assumes the configuration is kept.

choices.h: Either enantiomer, because the product is the same
choices.why: Each enantiomer gives a different enantiomer of the product. {{SN2}} does not pass through a planar intermediate.
An alcohol does not react: {{HO-}} is a strong base and a poor leaving group (lecture: N.R.).

steps.h: {{SN2}} inverts, so the starting material must have the opposite geometry at carbon 2.
Put Br on the face opposite the one SH is on in the product.
Br and SH are both rank 1 here, so the opposite geometry also has the opposite letter: R.

solution.rule: To choose a starting material, undo the inversion.

stem:
Draw the product with wedges and dashes and say whether it is cis or trans.
[[rxn:C[C@H]1CCC[C@H](Br)C1 + [SH-].[Na+]>DMSO;>"product"]]
model:
[[rxn:C[C@H]1CCC[C@H](Br)C1 + [SH-].[Na+]>DMSO;>C[C@H]1CCC[C@@H](S)C1 + [Na+].[Br-]]]

The starting material is trans. {{HS-}} attacks the carbon from the face opposite Br, so the product is cis-3-methylcyclohexanethiol.

rubric.h: SH on the carbon that carried Br
SH drawn on the opposite face to the one Br was on, methyl unchanged

steps.h: Br and the methyl group are on opposite faces: trans-1-bromo-3-methylcyclohexane.
Secondary bromide, {{HS-}} (126,000 in the lecture table), polar aprotic solvent: {{SN2}}.
SH goes on the opposite face to Br. The methyl carbon is untouched.
SH is now on the same face as the methyl group: cis.

stem:
(2S,3S)-2-Bromo-3-methylpentane reacts with NaSH in DMSO by {{SN2}}. What is the product?
[[mol:CC[C@H](C)[C@H](C)Br]]

choices.why: Carbon 2 is inverted and carbon 3 is exactly as it was: (2R,3S).
Retention at carbon 2: SH is drawn where Br was.
Both stereocentres were flipped. Carbon 3 is not attacked, so it cannot invert.
The wrong stereocentre was flipped: carbon 3 changed and carbon 2 did not.

steps.h: Carbon 2, the one bonded to Br. Carbon 3 is a stereocentre too, but it carries no leaving group.
SH goes on the face opposite Br at carbon 2. Carbon 3 keeps its drawing.
Carbon 2: SH > C3 > {{CH3}} > H with inverted geometry gives R. Carbon 3 is unchanged and still S: (2R,3S).

solution.rule: Only the carbon that loses the leaving group inverts.

stem: Which statement is true of every {{SN2}} reaction at a stereocentre?

choices.h: The nucleophile ends up on the face opposite the one the leaving group left from.
choices.why: This is backside attack, the third characteristic of {{SN2}} in lecture: inversion at the electrophile atom.

choices.h: An R starting material always gives an S product.
choices.why: Often, but not always. If the nucleophile has a different rank from the leaving group, the letter can stay the same even though the geometry inverted.

choices.h: The product is a racemic mixture.
choices.why: That is {{SN1}}, where a planar carbocation is attacked on both faces.

choices.h: Every stereocentre in the molecule is inverted.
choices.why: Only the carbon that carries the leaving group is attacked.

steps.h: Nucleophile, carbon and leaving group lie on one line. The nucleophile is on the side opposite the leaving group.
The geometry always inverts. The letter R or S depends on priorities, so it usually changes but does not have to.
There is no intermediate, so there is no racemization.

solution.answer: The nucleophile ends up on the face opposite the one the leaving group left from.
solution.rule: Always inversion of geometry. Usually, not always, a change of letter.

stem:
(S)-3-Bromo-3-methylhexane is stirred with NaCN in DMSO. What does the {{SN2}} reaction give?
[[mol:CCC[C@](C)(CC)Br]]

choices.h: No {{SN2}} product forms: the carbon is tertiary.
choices.why: The relative {{SN2}} rate of a tertiary substrate is 0 in the lecture table. Steric hindrance blocks the nucleophile.
This applies inversion without checking the substrate. Cyanide cannot reach the back of a tertiary carbon.
Retention, and at a tertiary carbon. {{SN2}} gives neither.

choices.h: A racemic mixture of the two nitriles, by {{SN2}}
choices.why: {{SN2}} never racemizes. A racemic product would mean a carbocation, which is {{SN1}}, not the reaction asked about.

steps.t: Classify the carbon before drawing anything
steps.h: The carbon with Br carries three carbon groups: it is tertiary.
Methyl > primary > secondary >>> tertiary. The lecture rate for a tertiary substrate is 0: the three groups block the back of the carbon.
No backside attack is possible, so there is no inverted nitrile to draw.

solution.answer: No SN2 product: the carbon is tertiary.
solution.rule: Check the substrate first. Tertiary means no SN2.

stem:
(S)-3-Bromotetrahydrofuran reacts with NaCN in DMSO. Which answer is correct?
[[mol:Br[C@H]1CCOC1]]

choices.why: CN is on the opposite face, and because the carbon next to oxygen outranks CN, the label remains S.
Right drawing, but the letter was flipped by habit. Ranking the product's groups gives S.
This is retention: CN on the same face as Br was. The letter changed only because the priorities changed.
Retention, and the label is wrong for this drawing as well.

steps.h:
Secondary carbon, good nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent: {{SN2}}. CN goes on the face opposite Br.
[[mol:N#C[C@@H]1CCOC1]]
Br > ring {{CH2}} bonded to O > the other ring {{CH2}} > H.
The ring {{CH2}} bonded to O carries (O, H, H) and CN carries (N, N, N). O beats N, so the ring {{CH2O}} is rank 1 and CN is rank 2.
Inverted geometry and swapped ranks 1 and 2: the letter is still S.

solution.answer: The inverted nitrile, which is still labelled S.
solution.rule: Inversion always. The letter only after ranking again.

stem:
A bottle of 2-bromobutane contains equal amounts of the R and S enantiomers. It reacts with NaSH in DMSO.
(a) Draw the product or products with stereochemistry.
(b) Is the product mixture optically active?
(c) Did inversion take place? Explain in one or two sentences.
model:
(a) [[rxn:CC[C@@H](C)Br + [SH-]>>CC[C@H](C)S + [Br-]]] [[rxn:CC[C@H](C)Br + [SH-]>>CC[C@@H](C)S + [Br-]]]

(b) No. The two thiols form in equal amounts (a racemic mixture), so the mixture is not optically active.

(c) Yes. Each molecule reacts by backside attack in one step, so R gives S and S gives R. The product is racemic because the starting material was racemic, not because a carbocation formed.

rubric.h: Both enantiomers of butane-2-thiol drawn, each from the bromide of opposite configuration
Says the product is racemic and not optically active
Says each molecule is inverted by backside attack, and that the racemic result comes from the racemic starting material, not from a carbocation

steps.h: {{SN2}} is one step for each molecule. The (R) bromide gives the (S) thiol and the (S) bromide gives the (R) thiol.
Equal amounts of the two bromides give equal amounts of the two thiols: a racemic product.
A racemic mixture does not rotate plane-polarized light.

steps.t: Separate the mechanism from the outcome
steps.h: Every molecule was inverted. The product is racemic only because the starting material was. This is not the racemization of {{SN1}}: no carbocation formed.

solution.answer: Both enantiomers of butane-2-thiol in equal amounts, not optically active, and every molecule reacted with inversion.
solution.rule: Racemic in, racemic out. Inversion still happens in every molecule.

stem:
(S)-Butane-2-thiol is treated with NaOH and then with {{CH3I}}. What is the product?
[[rxn:CC[C@H](C)S>1. NaOH;2. CH3I>"?"]]

choices.why: The stereocentre belongs to the nucleophile. No bond to it breaks, so its geometry is unchanged.
Inversion was applied to the wrong carbon. The carbon that is attacked is the methyl carbon of {{CH3I}}.
Nothing here makes the stereocentre planar, so it cannot racemize.
A thiolate is an excellent nucleophile and methyl iodide is the fastest {{SN2}} substrate.

steps.t: Step 1 is an acid and a base
steps.h: Hydroxide removes the S-H proton and gives the thiolate, {{RS-}}. No bond to the stereocentre changes.
The leaving group, iodide, is on the methyl carbon of {{CH3I}}. The thiolate is the nucleophile.
Inversion happens at the carbon that is attacked: the methyl carbon, which is not a stereocentre. The stereocentre is part of the nucleophile and none of its four bonds is broken.
The same geometry with {{SCH3}} in place of SH. S is still rank 1, so the label is still S.

solution.rule: Inversion happens at the electrophile's carbon, not in the nucleophile.
